summary: This standards-track document registers the media type example and example subtypes in the standards tree. The example/* and */example media types are for use in documentation only.

plainLanguage.summary: When writing a guide, you need a pretend file type that cannot be confused with a real one. This reserves the word example for that.

questions: what is the example media type
can i implement example/* media types
subtitle: A reserved pretend media type, so documentation examples can never be mistaken for real requirements.

tldr.problem: Documents often show examples that use a media type where the actual type does not matter, and readers or implementers may mistake the example for a requirement.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers an 'example' media type and an 'example' subtype under eight existing types (application, audio, image, message, model, multipart, text and video) in the standards tree, all for documentation only.
tldr.outcome: Authors get names whose illustrative role is obvious. Implementations MUST NOT implement them, and real use leads to interoperability problems.

facts.label: Subtype registrations
facts.value: 8 (application, audio, image, message, model, multipart, text, video)

today: RFC 4735 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the registration for the example media type and subtypes.

sections.title: Why Examples Need a Safe Name
sections.content:
Documents from the IETF and other standards bodies sometimes show examples that involve a media type, where the actual type is not relevant. In those cases it helps to show a type whose illustrative role is clear.

The RFC notes that in the worst case this helps to debug implementations where the designer mistook the example for a requirement of the protocol concerned. It also suggests that people writing examples with media types in trees other than the standards tree might include the string example in their hypothetical types.
sections.plainLanguage: If a recipe says 'use flour type X' as a pretend example, a cook might think X is real. A silly, obviously pretend name stops that mix-up.

sections.title: What Gets Registered
sections.content:
The RFC registers two things in the standards tree, following the rules of RFC 4288.

  • The top-level example media type.
  • The subtype example under eight existing types: application, audio, image, message, model, multipart, text and video.

So text/example and video/example are valid placeholders when a document needs a text or video type, and example/* works when even the top-level type is irrelevant.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a pretend label for every kind of file the document mentions: pretend picture, pretend sound, pretend video, and so on.

sections.title: Rules for the example Type
sections.content:
Any subtype may be used with the example type, but IANA MUST NOT register any subtypes for it. Its parameters and encoding considerations are 'as invented by the user', since nothing real is behind it.

The registration lists the intended usage as LIMITED USE. It is intended only for documents giving examples of specifying some media type where the actual type used is irrelevant. The author and change controller are the Internet Engineering Task Force.
sections.plainLanguage: The pretend label is yours to fill in however you like for a story, but the librarian is not allowed to add any real books under it.

sections.title: Rules for the example Subtypes
sections.content:
For the eight */example subtypes, required parameters are those required by the type plus any others invented by the user. Optional parameters are those offered by the type plus any others invented by the user.

As with the top-level type, usage is LIMITED USE, meant only for documents giving examples of some subtype of the given media type, where the actual subtype is irrelevant.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pretend label follows the normal rules of its kind of file, and you may make up extra details for your story.

sections.title: Do Not Implement These
sections.content:
The RFC is firm that the example type and subtypes are defined for documentation only. They MUST NOT be implemented. Their appearance in real code could lead to unpredictable results and thus potentially open up security holes.

On interoperability, any attempt to negotiate or send one of these types is bound to lead to interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A pretend label is for stories only. If a real machine starts using it, nobody can predict what will happen.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
The document itself is the registration. It specifies and registers the example media type and the application/example, audio/example, image/example, message/example, model/example, multipart/example, text/example and video/example subtypes.

The contact address given for further information is ietf-types@iana.org.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list keeper wrote these pretend names down so that nobody else claims them for something real.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
Freed, N. and J. Klensin, "Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures", BCP 13, RFC 4288, December 2005.
